Nābhi
------------------------------------------
He was the son of the king आग्नीध्र and Vipracitti. Priyavrata was his grandfather. His wife was Merudevī and the great king ऋषभ was his son and successor.
The kingdom (or the country) ruled by him came to be known as Nābhivarṣa or Ajanābhavarṣa, same as भारतवर्ष.

-1700)
------------------------------------------
Great saints have been the ‘salt of the earth’ in India. Narration of their lives has been considered as an act of great religious merit.
It goes to the credit of नाभादास that he has preserved for the posterity, the detailed lives of about two hundred minstrels of God, in his now well-known book Bhaktamālā or Bhaktamālikā.
Born perhaps in A.

at the village राम-bhadrācala, on the bank of the river गोदावरी (in Andhra Pradesh) to रामदास, himself a great devotee of राम, he lost his ड़थेर् at an early age and was abandoned by his मोथेर् due to extreme poverty. The child was adopted by one Agradāsa, by name, belonging to Galatā near Jaipur (in Rajasthan). Agradāsa too seems to have been a saint and is said to have initiated the child into the cult of devotion to राम, with the new name ‘Nābhādāsa,’ the original name being Nārāyaṇadāsa.
Nābhādāsa was well-educated and endowed with great poetical talents. He was also a humble devotee of God.
His work Bhaktamālā is written in Hindi (Brajbhāṣā) poetry in the metre called ‘Chappa’ (with six lines). The language is elegant though full of Sanskrit words.
There are many commentaries on this work as also several other Bhaktamālās by other writers, who have kept this work as their model.

Nābhānediṣṭha
(‘nearest in birth or descent’)
------------------------------------------
The Ṛgveda is the oldest scripture in the world. One of the important ṛṣis or sages of this Veda to whom are attributed 38 ṛks (Ṛgvedic mantras) (10.6

) is नाभानेदिष्ठ. He was the last son of the sage मनु.
There is an interesting story about him (vide ऐतरेय Brāhmaṇa 22.14 and Taittirīya Saṁhitā

.4 to 7). When he was in the गुरुकुल for एदुचतिओन्, his elder brothers divided all the paternal property among themselves leaving nothing for him! After he returned home, he requested his ड़थेर् मनु for his share of the property. मनु asked him to go to the sage अङ्गिरस् who was performing a सत्त्रयाग but did not know the mantras to be chanted on the sixth day. Nābhāne-diṣṭha, who knew these mantras, could offer his services, win his confidence, as also plenty of money (or property).
Everything happened as मनु had predicted. However, when नाभानेदिष्ठ was about to take the thousand cows given to him by the sage अङ्गिरस्, रुद्र (Śiva) appeared on the scene and claimed them as his, as per the rules of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्. When मनु, who was apprised of this, concurred with रुद्र and नाभानेदिष्ठ told him the truth, रुद्र was pleased with his devotion to truth and gave away all the cows. According to another version, the sage pleased रुद्र by performing a ritual called ‘Manthisaṁsrāva.’
